stimulus.title: Literary Narrative: Night Ferry
stimulus.text:
The ferry left the mainland at eleven, and by the time it cleared the breakwater, Teo was the only passenger still on the open deck. The others had gone inside, where the benches were warm and a television bolted to the ceiling showed a game no one was watching. He preferred the cold. After nine months of dormitory radiators that clanked all night and a roommate who slept with the window shut, the wind off the strait felt like something he had been owed.

He had imagined this crossing many times during the spring, usually in the middle of an exam. In the imagined version he stood at the rail exactly as he was standing now, and the lights of the island rose out of the dark one by one, and he felt the whole year fall away from him like a coat he no longer needed. What he had not imagined was how small the lights would look. From the dormitory, the island had seemed enormous, the place where everything important had happened. From the deck, it looked like a handful of sparks someone had forgotten to put out.

“You're Ana Reyes's boy.” The voice came from behind him, and Teo turned to find a man in oil-stained coveralls leaning in the doorway of the engine room, wiping his hands on a rag that was dirtier than his hands. Teo recognized him vaguely, the way he recognized most adults on the island: as part of the scenery, like the church steeple or the tide charts posted outside the post office. “Hollis,” the man said. “I've run the engines on this boat since before you were born. Your mother used to ride out with her algebra homework. Never once finished it before we docked.”

Teo laughed, surprised. His mother taught math at the island's only school now, and the idea of her as a girl struggling with equations on a rolling deck seemed both impossible and entirely obvious. Hollis came to stand beside him at the rail. For a while neither of them spoke. The engines thudded beneath their feet with a steadiness Teo could feel in his teeth.

“So,” Hollis said eventually. “Is it what you expected? The mainland?” Teo started to give the answer he had been giving all year, on the phone to his parents and in messages to friends who had stayed behind: that it was great, that he was busy, that the library was open until two in the morning. But the dark made it easier to say something truer. “It's bigger,” he said. “Everyone there is from somewhere else, so nobody asks where you're from. I thought I'd like that more than I did.”

Hollis nodded as if this were information about the weather. “Your mother said the same thing, near enough, the first summer she came back.” He folded the rag into a neat square and tucked it into his pocket. “She said the trouble with leaving is that you change, and the trouble with coming back is that the island doesn't. Then she said she was wrong about the second part.”

“Wrong how?” Teo asked. Hollis shrugged. “Island changes, too. Just slower. Harbor's been dredged twice since you were little. The bakery's under new owners, and they put walnuts in everything now, which some people consider a crime. Old Mrs. Petrakis finally retired from the post office.” He paused. “Thing is, when you live here, you don't see it happening. You need to go away for a while before you can notice.”

The lights of the harbor had grown larger as they talked, and now Teo could pick out individual shapes: the floodlit fuel dock, the red blink of the channel marker, the square yellow windows of houses along the hill where people were still awake. One of those windows, he knew, was his own kitchen, where his mother would be sitting with a cup of tea she had let go cold, pretending not to wait for him.

Hollis pushed himself away from the rail. “Engines don't watch themselves,” he said, and disappeared below. Teo stayed where he was. The island was no longer a handful of sparks. It was not enormous, either. It was simply the size it was, and for the first time all year he thought he might be able to see it clearly.

Teo recognized him vaguely, the way he recognized most adults on the island: as part of the scenery, like the church steeple or the tide charts posted outside the post office. “Hollis,” the man said. “I've run the engines on this boat since before you were born. Old Mrs. Petrakis finally retired from the post office.” He paused. “Thing is, when you live here, you don't see it happening. You need to go away for a while before you can notice.”

One of those windows, he knew, was his own kitchen, where his mother would be sitting with a cup of tea she had let go cold, pretending not to wait for him.

Hollis pushed himself away from the rail. “Engines don't watch themselves,” he said, and disappeared below. Teo stayed where he was. The island was no longer a handful of sparks. It was not enormous, either. It was simply the size it was, and for the first time all year he thought he might be able to see it clearly.

prompt: The passage suggests that Teo's mother, as she waits in the kitchen, is:

choices.text: annoyed that the ferry is running later than scheduled
choices.rationale: No delay or annoyance is mentioned.

choices.text: eager for Teo's return but reluctant to let it show
choices.rationale: Correct. She has let her tea go cold while “pretending not to wait for him.”

choices.text: busy preparing tomorrow's lessons for her students
choices.rationale: Lesson planning is never mentioned.

choices.text: unaware that her son is coming home on this ferry
choices.rationale: Teo knows she is waiting, so she knows he is coming.

explanation: Paragraph 8: a cold cup of tea and “pretending not to wait” show restrained eagerness.
